# the SDM explore page

Sixteen lines of SETTLE build the machine. The program calls the read-address `read-address:`; Kanerva calls it the retrieval address, or the retrieval cue. `address-noise: 0.1` flips a tenth of its bits.

Look at the last two lines: an address that was never written (:zebra) and pure noise both come back as :cat. In a memory this small the basins cover most of the cube. Experiment 3 refuses such reads.

## Pick an address and watch it answer (1 · LIVE · THE MACHINE)

Pick a start on the left: a stored pattern with some of its bits flipped (a **noisy address**), a word that was never stored, or pure noise. The hard locations within 12 bits of the address wake and vote, and the answer appears on the right. Press RUN and the answer becomes the next address, until the read gives back what it was given. Press an address bit to flip it, or hold it.

Each hard-location has a fixed random 32-bit address and 32 bit-counters. The three stars are the stored patterns, :cat :dog :owl, drawn at their distance from the address.

## How a read works (HOW IT WORKS · ONE IDEA AT A TIME)

The distance between two words is the number of bits where they differ. A hard location wakes when its address is within the activation radius. With 64 random addresses and activation radius 12, about five wake for any address.

THE VOTE panel under the diagram shows it. Each woken hard-location is a row of 32 bit-counters, rose for positive and indigo for negative. The sums are the bars; the sign of each bar is one bit of the answer. The amber ring marks a tie.

Turn the temperature up in the diagram. At T = 0 a bit takes the sign of its sum. Warm, it is a weighted coin, SETTLE's p-bit: a big sum still almost always wins, a small sum is a near toss-up. The memory holds its pattern when warm and melts when hot.

Kanerva 1993 gives the capacity as a share of the hard locations, where φ is the chance a stored bit is read back right from its exact address. At φ = 0.999 it is 0.105 words per hard location as the memory grows without end, and 0.096 for his million-location sample memory. KANERVA’s theory module reproduces both numbers in its tests. A noisy address holds fewer.

## Experiments you can run in this tab (EXPERIMENTS · SETTLE × KANERVA)

Each one runs the memory here and sets its result beside a recorded or sealed number. They show where the memory holds, where it melts, and what a **key** or a **refusal rule** does to a read.

Experiment 2 sets the S-map’s prediction beside the count. The plain map is optimistic once the address-noise reaches 30%: at a million hard locations it predicted 1,648 words at 30% noise where 700 were measured. KANERVA’s TRACK prediction follows the measured recall (the KANERVA page shows both).
